items.claim: The shift to the wider diaspora as subject at 40:11, closing on the petuchah after 40:12, is an adequately warranted and honestly calibrated scene seam.
items.evidence: Both verses' Hebrew and English quotations are complete and verbatim against the folded text. The closing mark at the span's end verse is correctly typed as a petuchah rather than conflated with a setumah, and disclosed single-witness; the paseq at the opening verse is correctly cited as count-only. The front seam is genuinely soft -- no formula marks the turn from the field captains to the wider diaspora -- and the wine-and-summer-fruit catchword pairing that straddles the seam back to the captains' own instruction is disclosed as live cohesion rather than left as a silent echo. The row's medium_low confidence with the frontier flag honestly reflects that softness rather than sitting at an unexamined high.

items.claim: The curly-quoted WEB rendering paired with the byte splice for 40:14 is truncated against the staged folded text, dropping the verse's second clause.
items.evidence: This verse carries a live continuation-paragraph fold, and its full folded text runs the reported warning through a second sentence, “But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam didn’t believe them.” (web:Jer.40.14). The row's own Hebrew splice for the verse correctly carries that second clause in full, but the WEB quotation offered as its match stops at the end of the direct-speech warning and never renders the disbelief clause, so the Hebrew-to-English match claimed for this verse is not actually same-span. This does not disturb the row's own boundaries, since both clauses fall inside the span either way, and the setumah, ketiv/qere, and paseq disclosures elsewhere in the row check out correctly against the marked-verse inventory. The gap sits exactly at a verse separately flagged as a live fold hazard, where fidelity is judged against the staged folded text rather than a naive per-sentence read.

items.claim: The month-notice onset at 41:1 and the fresh date notice at 41:4 both carry the row's boundaries cleanly, and the row is careful not to fold the month notice into the book's reign-year date-formula inventory.
items.evidence: All three verses' quotations are complete and verbatim against the folded text. The setumah closing the prior chapter and the paseq markers inside this span are correctly typed and disclosed single-witness. The rejected alternative -- folding this unit into the pilgrim massacre that follows as one continuous killing spree -- is a real rival, not a strawman, given the same actor drives both episodes, and it is adequately answered by the fresh date notice naming an entirely new, previously unmentioned party at the far seam. The device notes correctly distinguish this calendar marker from the bishnat/bashanah reign-year shape rather than over-claiming membership in that inventory.

items.claim: The curly-quoted WEB rendering paired with the byte splice for 41:8 is truncated against the staged folded text, and the same partial-quotation pattern recurs at other verses in this span that are not fold sites at all.
items.evidence: 41:8 carries a live continuation-paragraph fold; its full folded text runs the ten men's plea through a second sentence, “So he stopped, and didn’t kill them among their brothers.” (web:Jer.41.8). The row's own Hebrew splice for the verse carries that second clause in full, but the paired WEB quotation stops at the plea itself and never renders the sparing clause, so the claimed match is not same-span at a verse specifically flagged as a fold hazard requiring judgment against the staged folded text. The row's own disclosure at this verse addresses only the paragraph break's tier-4 status, not the separate quotation gap. The same pattern -- a full Hebrew byte splice paired with only part of the corresponding English sentence -- recurs at 41:6, where the quotation renders only Ishmael's spoken line and omits the narrated frame that is part of the same verse, and at 41:9, where the Hebrew splice has no paired WEB quotation at all. This is inconsistent with this row's own full-verse practice at 41:4, 41:5, 41:7, and 41:10, and with the full-verse-to-full-verse pairing used throughout the assassination account at 41:1-41:3.

items.claim: The named-figure onset at 41:11 and the recap-opening seam before 41:16 both carry clean, verbatim-quoted boundaries, and the rejected alternative honestly engages the recap's continued grammatical subject rather than dismissing it.
items.evidence: All five verses in the span are quoted in full and verbatim against the folded text, with no truncation at any internal clause boundary. The closing setumah at the prior verse is correctly typed and disclosed single-witness. The rejected alternative -- reading the following recap as a continuation of the rescue narrative, since the same named figure remains the grammatical subject across the seam -- is a genuine rival rather than a strawman, and the row's answer, that the recap opens a fresh summarizing movement rather than continuing the chase, holds against the verse's own content.

items.claim: The exclusivity claim that the place-name at 41:17 is named only here in the book lacks the digit-bearing sweep citation this same claim-type correctly carries elsewhere in this span.
items.evidence: The device notes assert the toponym is named only here in the book but attach no sweep count to that claim, unlike the parallel only-here-in-the-book claim made for the Ammonite king at 40:14, which correctly appends a one-verse sweep count to the identical claim-type. The underlying exclusivity claim is plausible on the bytes actually cited, but as written it falls exactly in the claim class held to a hard standard: an adjacent digit-bearing citation naming the swept object and unit is required, and the ketiv/qere disclosure alone does not supply it. The row's seam warrants at both ends are otherwise sound: the recap-opening front seam and the setumah-marked, ketiv/qere-disclosed interior verses check out against the marked-verse inventory, and the back seam correctly identifies the fresh collective-subject onset that opens the next scene.
